summary:
Merge sort: split the array in half, sort each half the same way, and merge the two sorted halves by
repeatedly taking the smaller front value. Every level of splitting does O(n) merging and there are log n
levels, so it's O(n log n) on every input.

question.md:
Sort up to 10⁵ integers (negative ones included) from lowest to highest, **without** the language's built-in
sort.

- **Duplicates** are allowed and must all be kept.
- **10⁵ values** rule out O(n²) sorts: that's up to 10¹⁰ steps.

think.md:
Take `[42, -7, 15, 42, 0, 9]`. Sorted: `[-7, 0, 9, 15, 42, 42]`.

The simple idea (insert each value into a sorted prefix) costs up to n steps per value. To do better, use the
fact that **merging two sorted lists is cheap**: compare their fronts and take the smaller, n steps for n
values. If we can get two sorted halves, one merge finishes the job; and each half can be sorted the same way.

approaches.title: Insertion sort

idea.md: Keep the first `i` values sorted. Take value `i`, shift every bigger value in the prefix one place right, and drop it into the gap.

build: For each `i ≥ 1`, hold `x = a[i]` and walk `j` left while `a[j] > x`, shifting.

lines.text: `a[0..i-1]` is sorted; take the next value `x`.
Every bigger value in the prefix moves one place right, opening a gap.
`x` drops into the gap: the prefix is sorted again, one longer.
The whole array is the prefix now.

complexity.md: **Time O(n²)** in the worst case (a reversed array shifts everything every time), O(n) if already sorted. **Space O(n)** for the copy.

steps.text: The first score alone is a sorted prefix.
Insert -7: it slides past 1 bigger score(s) and lands at position 0.
Insert 15: it slides past 1 bigger score(s) and lands at position 1.
Insert 42: it slides past 0 bigger score(s) and lands at position 3.
Insert 0: it slides past 3 bigger score(s) and lands at position 1.
Insert 9: it slides past 3 bigger score(s) and lands at position 2.

walk.title: Insertion sort: grow a sorted prefix; each new score slides left past every bigger score.

limits.md: Up to 5 × 10⁹ shifts for 10⁵ scores. Sorting halves and merging them avoids comparing values that are far apart one by one.

approaches.title: Quick sort with a random pivot

idea.md: Pick a random pivot, partition so smaller values come first and the pivot sits in its final place, then quick-sort the two sides. A random pivot splits the range reasonably evenly on average.

build: Recursive `sort(lo, hi)`: stop when the range has fewer than 2 values.
Swap a random element to `hi` as the pivot.
Partition: walk `j` over the range, moving values smaller than the pivot to the front.
Put the pivot after them and recurse on both sides.

lines.text: Sort `a[lo..hi]`; a range of 0 or 1 values is already sorted.
A random pivot, moved to the end of the range. Randomness makes a terrible split unlikely, whatever the input order.
`a[lo..i-1]` holds the values smaller than the pivot found so far; each smaller `a[j]` is swapped into that region.
The pivot goes right after the smaller values: that's its final sorted position.

complexity.md: **Time O(n log n) expected**, O(n²) in the unlucky worst case. **Space O(log n)** expected for the recursion.

steps.text: Positions 0..5: pivot 9 (the last one, for this walkthrough). Smaller values go left; 9 lands at position 2, its final place.
Positions 0..1: pivot 0 (the last one, for this walkthrough). Smaller values go left; 0 lands at position 1, its final place.
Positions 3..5: pivot 15 (the last one, for this walkthrough). Smaller values go left; 15 lands at position 3, its final place.
Positions 4..5: pivot 42 (the last one, for this walkthrough). Smaller values go left; 42 lands at position 4, its final place.

walk.title: Quick sort: pick a pivot, move smaller values to its left and larger ones to its right, then sort both sides the same way.

limits.md: Only fast on average: an unlucky run of pivots (or many equal values, which all land on one side) degrades it to O(n²) with deep recursion. Merge sort guarantees O(n log n) on every input.

approaches.title: Merge sort

idea.md: Sort the left half and the right half (recursively), then merge them: compare the two front values, take the smaller (the left one on ties, which keeps equal values in order), and repeat until both halves are used up.

build: `sort(lo, hi)` on a half-open range; stop at length 1.
Merge into a buffer with two pointers, then copy the buffer back.

lines.text: A copy to sort and one buffer, reused by every merge.
Sort the half-open range `[lo, hi)`; one value is already sorted.
Both halves are sorted, so the smallest remaining value is one of the two fronts. `<=` takes the left one on ties, which keeps the sort stable.
One half ran out; the rest of the other is already sorted and bigger than everything taken.
Copy the merged range back into place.

complexity.md: **Time O(n log n)** on every input: log n levels of halving, O(n) merging per level. **Space O(n)** for the buffer, plus O(log n) recursion.

walk.title: Merge sort: split in half until pieces have one value, then merge sorted pieces back together, always taking the smaller front value.

takeaways.md:
- **Merge sort** guarantees O(n log n) and is stable; **quick sort** is in place and fast on average, but only with
  a good pivot.
- Merging two sorted lists takes linear time: that's the heart of many problems (counting inversions, sorting
  linked lists, k-way merges).
- Know when a quadratic sort is fine (tiny or nearly sorted inputs) and when it isn't.
